Yes. After reading `CURRENT.md`, tracing the live Builder/Pipeline code, and looking through the papers in your research zip, I think the answer is pretty clear:

**Do not treat video as “Stage 1 + Stage 2 for carousels, but with more fields.”**  
Video needs a **different grammar model**, although the underlying philosophy you already established-observation first, canonical taxonomy, explicit constraints, compiler, deterministic runtime-is exactly the right foundation.

And I would **not start with fine-tuning**.

I would start by learning how the research community decomposes *editing itself* into observable, composable units, then build your own **Video Visual Syntax IR** around that.

---

# 1. The most important thing I found in your current system

Your existing Stage 1/Stage 2 work is actually a very strong starting point.

You already have:

**Stage 1**
> specimen → visual observations → canonical primitives/zones/roles

**Stage 2**
> observations → normalized composition specification → locks/anchors/constraints → validated spec

And this is genuinely implemented, not merely a PRD concept. `CURRENT.md` records 49/49 Stage 2 passes, with the taxonomy normalization rejecting noncanonical values rather than silently accepting them.

But the current Stage 2 compiler is fundamentally **spatial/static**. Its grammar revolves around things like:

- `slide_role`
- zones
- primitive types
- attribute ranges
- anchor modes
- cross-slide anchors
- spatial wrong-reading locks

That is exactly right for your carousel/supervisual problem.

Video introduces a new dimension:

> **the grammar happens over time.**

And the current Pipeline runtime reflects that.

Your `VideoEditProgramService` has a canonical timeline made of tracks and timed elements such as `SOURCE_SEGMENT`, `TEXT`, `MOTION_SLOT`, `GENERATED_SLOT`, etc. The `WordBoundaryEdlService` is particularly mature: it knows word boundaries, source ranges, output ranges, cut-in/out classes and authorized reordering.

But this runtime is still essentially:

> **semantic selection → timeline/EDL → FFmpeg**

rather than:

> **reference video → editing grammar → structured temporal composition → renderer**

That distinction matters enormously.

---

# 2. What I would make your research curriculum

From the papers you supplied, I would divide them into **four levels**.

| Priority | Paper | Why it matters to you |
|---|---|---|
| **#1** | **VEU-Bench** | Gives you the closest thing in the corpus to an ontology of editing language |
| **#2** | **Edit3K** | Shows how to represent *editing components themselves*, rather than just video content |
| **#3** | **AutoTransition** | Teaches the problem of learning relationships between neighboring shots |
| **#4** | **V-Trans4Style** | Important for turning “style” into observable transition/editing behavior |
| **#5** | **CutClaw** | Useful for the eventual agent/compiler architecture |
| **#6** | **AutoCut** | Useful later for learned tokenization + controllable generation |
| **#7** | **Vidi** | Strong for your already-solved-ish semantic/media retrieval layer |
| **#8** | **OmniShotCut** | Useful for the low-level segmentation boundary of your temporal grammar |
| **#9** | **IVEBench** | Very useful once you start evaluating reproduction |
| **#10** | **Self-SiMS / zero-shot moment retrieval** | Mostly relevant to the old Format01 scene-finding problem |

The first four are the ones I would actually **study deeply**.

---

# 3. #1 - VEU-Bench

## This is the paper I would start with.

**VEU-Bench: Towards Comprehensive Understanding of Video Editing**

It is unusually aligned with what you are trying to build because it does not just ask:

> “What is happening in the video?”

It asks:

> **“What editing operation is happening, what does it look like, why is it used, and can a model judge it?”**

The benchmark explicitly decomposes editing into dimensions including intra-frame properties such as shot size and inter-shot attributes such as cut types and transitions. More importantly, it organizes tasks into **recognition → reasoning → judging** rather than stopping at classification. ([CVF Open Access](https://openaccess.thecvf.com/content/CVPR2025/html/Li_VEU-Bench_Towards_Comprehensive_Understanding_of_Video_Editing_CVPR_2025_paper.html?utm_source=chatgpt.com))

That is almost exactly the missing conceptual layer in your current project.

### Why this is extremely relevant to you

Your Stage 1 currently asks something like:

> What objects/zones/primitives are visible?

The video equivalent needs to ask:

> **What editorial operation caused this visual state?**

For example:

```text
SHOT_01
  shot_size = medium
  subject = speaker
  camera = static

CUT_01
  type = hard_cut
  function = emphasis

SHOT_02
  shot_size = close_up
  subject = speaker
  framing_change = tighter

TEXT_EVENT_01
  type = keyword_emphasis
  onset = aligned_to_word("failure")

MOTION_EVENT_01
  type = punch_in
  duration = 280ms

AUDIO_RELATION_01
  type = L_CUT
```

That is much closer to a **visual syntax** than “there is a person and some text.”

VEU-Bench also matters because it explicitly treats editing knowledge as an **ontology**, using an ontology-based annotation pipeline to turn abstract editing concepts into video-specific observations. ([CVF Open Access](https://openaccess.thecvf.com/content/CVPR2025/papers/Li_VEU-Bench_Towards_Comprehensive_Understanding_of_Video_Editing_CVPR_2025_paper.pdf?utm_source=chatgpt.com))

### What I would study

Don't read it as “another benchmark.”

Read it as:

> **How do I construct the vocabulary of my video grammar?**

Extract every dimension/table/ontology it uses and compare it against your own five formats.

---

# 4. #2 - Edit3K

This one might actually be even more important for the *engineering* side.

**Edit3K: Universal Representation Learning for Video Editing Components**

Its central insight is very compatible with your ambition:

> don't learn representations of *videos* alone; learn representations of the **editing components applied to videos**.

The authors build a dataset around approximately **3,094 editing components and 618,800 rendered videos**, with atomic components including effects, animation, transitions, filters, stickers and text. The crucial idea is to isolate the visual signature of the editing component from the underlying source material. ([arXiv](https://arxiv.org/abs/2403.16048?utm_source=chatgpt.com))

That is basically the question you're asking.

Suppose you have:

```text
speaker talking
```

and five references:

```text
speaker + punch-in
speaker + punch-in + typography
speaker + punch-in + freeze-frame
speaker + punch-in + image overlay
speaker + punch-in + kinetic caption
```

You don't want your model to conclude that those are five unrelated visual objects.

You want it to learn:

```text
BASE_SHOT

+ PUNCH_IN
+ KINETIC_CAPTION
+ IMAGE_OVERLAY
+ FREEZE_FRAME
```

Those are **operations**.

That is a completely different representation strategy.

### This suggests something important for your harnesses

Your future taxonomy should probably contain at least three layers:

```text
CONTENT
    speaker
    b-roll
    screenshot
    quote
    product
    archival_clip

EDITORIAL_OPERATION
    hard_cut
    J_cut
    L_cut
    punch_in
    crop_reframe
    split_screen
    freeze
    speed_ramp
    overlay
    typography_reveal
    mask
    transition
    etc.

FUNCTION
    emphasis
    contrast
    reveal
    acceleration
    interruption
    proof
    emotional_release
    anticipation
```

That third layer is where Format01 starts becoming very valuable.

More on that below.

---

# 5. #3 - AutoTransition

**AutoTransition: Learning to Recommend Video Transition Effects**

This is a very good paper for understanding that editing syntax isn't merely a bag of independent operations.

Transitions depend on:

> **what came before + what comes next + audio + context.**

The authors formulate transition recommendation as multimodal retrieval and explicitly model sequential context between neighboring transition decisions. ([arXiv](https://arxiv.org/abs/2207.13479?utm_source=chatgpt.com))

That should immediately resonate with your architecture.

A naïve grammar says:

```text
SHOT_A
CUT
SHOT_B
```

A useful grammar says:

```text
SHOT_A
    ↓
semantic relationship
    ↓
visual relationship
    ↓
audio relationship
    ↓
transition operator
    ↓
SHOT_B
```

For example:

```text
A_ROLL assertion
→ abrupt conceptual contradiction
→ ironic found clip
→ HARD_CUT + AUDIO_STAB
```

That's an **editing production rule**.

And now you're getting somewhere interesting.

---

# 6. #4 - V-Trans4Style

This one is especially relevant to your phrase:

> “I want the model to understand our editing format and reproduce it without fail.”

**V-Trans4Style** explicitly studies production style adaptation via visual transition patterns.

It doesn't treat “style” purely as a prose prompt. It learns sequences of transitions and introduces style conditioning, with the explicit goal of making the resulting transition sequences match a target production style. ([ECCV 2026](https://eccv.ecva.net/virtual/2024/poster/662?utm_source=chatgpt.com))

That is conceptually very close to what you are calling a **format**.

Your five video formats shouldn't eventually just be:

```yaml
format: format_03
```

They should become something closer to:

```yaml
format:
    grammar_family: silent_dialogue_theatre

    temporal_rhythm:
       avg_shot_duration: ...
       variance: ...

    transition_distribution:
       hard_cut: ...
       match_cut: ...
       dissolve: ...

    shot_progression:
       wide -> medium -> close
       ...

    typography:
       entry: ...
       persistence: ...
       emphasis: ...

    audio_video_relations:
       ...

    recurrence_rules:
       ...
```

That's **style as executable syntax**, not style as a prompt.

---

# 7. #5 - CutClaw

Now we get into architecture.

CutClaw is less useful for defining the taxonomy, but very useful for understanding how you might eventually **execute** it.

The system decomposes long-form editing into structured stages, including hierarchical multimodal decomposition, a planning component, shot-point selection, and collaborative editor/reviewer agents. ([arXiv](https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.29664?utm_source=chatgpt.com))

The important architectural lesson isn't “build agents.”

It's:

> **don't have one model directly generate the final video.**

Instead:

```text
observe
   ↓
plan
   ↓
compose
   ↓
validate
   ↓
repair
   ↓
render
```

Which is remarkably consistent with your existing constitutional architecture.

Your existing pipeline already wants this kind of distinction.

So I would borrow **the decomposition**, not necessarily the exact agent implementation.

---

# 8. #6 - AutoCut

AutoCut is where things become interesting for the longer-term learned system.

The 2026 CVPR paper uses multimodal discretization to place video, audio and text into a shared discrete space, then uses a multimodal model to predict/edit token sequences that are ultimately rendered. ([CVF Open Access](https://openaccess.thecvf.com/content/CVPR2026/papers/Zhou_AutoCut_End-to-end_advertisement_video_editing_based_on_multimodal_discretization_and_CVPR_2026_paper.pdf?utm_source=chatgpt.com))

That is extremely relevant to your eventual:

> embeddings / DSPy / fine-tuning / whatever gets the job done

question.

But I would **not start here**.

Because AutoCut makes much more sense once you've already discovered what your tokens/operations actually mean.

Otherwise you'll have:

> a very clever latent representation of a taxonomy you haven't correctly defined.

Your problem today is much more like **representation engineering** than model scaling.

---

# 9. #7 - Vidi

Vidi is very useful-but mostly for a problem you already partially solved with Format01.

Its first release focuses heavily on temporal retrieval over long videos, including hour-long inputs, multimodal queries, and retrieval of relevant time ranges. ([arXiv](https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.15681?utm_source=chatgpt.com))

This is excellent for:

```text
"find me the moment where..."
```

which sounds very close to what your Format01 system originally did.

And your old Format01 library confirms this.

You have:

- 60 historical scene templates
- 25 active runtime scene templates
- scene categories such as `HOOK`, `SETUP`, `CHALLENGE`, `TURNING_POINT`, `RESOLUTION`, `VISION`
- A-roll/B-roll/C-roll patterns
- J/L-cuts
- match cuts
- symbolic echoes
- contrast
- tease
- truth
- effects

That is **not useless at all**.

But it is primarily a **semantic/narrative scene grammar**.

It answers:

> What should the next scene do?

It doesn't sufficiently answer:

> What exact temporal/spatial/motion/audio operations make that scene look like our house style?

So I would *not throw Format01 away*.

I would demote it one layer:

```text
FORMAT01 SCENE LANGUAGE
        ↓
semantic scene intent
        ↓
VIDEO VISUAL SYNTAX
        ↓
temporal composition
        ↓
runtime program
```

That's the correct relationship.

---

# 10. #8 - OmniShotCut

This one is lower priority but very practical.

OmniShotCut treats shot boundary detection as a structured relational problem and detects not just clean cuts but transitions such as dissolve, wipe and fade across diverse video domains. ([GitHub](https://github.com/UVA-Computer-Vision-Lab/OmniShotCut?utm_source=chatgpt.com))

Why I care about this for you:

Your future Stage 1 needs a reliable primitive like:

```text
SHOT_BOUNDARY
```

before it can infer higher-level grammar.

Otherwise you're asking an LMM to hallucinate the temporal units it is supposed to reason over.

So I would use a combination of:

```text
shot detector
+
audio segmentation
+
frame-difference/motion probes
+
MLLM/VLM
```

rather than asking one model to watch the entire video and “tell us the grammar.”

---

# 11. #9 - IVEBench

This one becomes important once you have your compiler.

IVEBench is useful because it treats instruction-guided editing as something that needs **systematic evaluation**, with eight editing categories, 35 subcategories, and a three-dimensional evaluation protocol covering video quality, instruction compliance and fidelity. ([Hugging Face](https://huggingface.co/papers/2510.11647?utm_source=chatgpt.com))

This maps nicely onto the question:

> “did we reproduce the reference format?”

because visual similarity alone isn't enough.

You eventually need:

```text
Semantic fidelity
+
Structural fidelity
+
Temporal fidelity
+
Visual fidelity
+
Format fidelity
```

The last one is the one your current system is missing.

---

# 12. The paper I would *not* prioritize: Self-SiMS

The zero-shot moment-retrieval paper is interesting. It specifically attacks the gap between text-language style and video similarity and introduces self-similarity-based proposal/scoring. ([arXiv](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.19027?utm_source=chatgpt.com))

But this is mostly the **old Format01 problem**:

> find the right footage.

You are now saying:

> **we know what content we want; we need the system to reproduce how our format edits it.**

Different problem.

So I'd understand it later, but not put it at the center of your visual-syntax curriculum.

---

# 13. What I would NOT spend much time on from this particular folder

The following are interesting but peripheral to your immediate problem:

**LayTextLLM / bounding-box work**  
Useful inspiration for turning spatial relationships into compact structured representations, but it comes from document understanding rather than temporal editing.

**BBQ-to-Image / bounding-box diffusion**  
Potentially valuable much later for controlled asset generation, but not for discovering editing grammar.

**Bounding Box Stability**  
Not central.

**Bounding Box-Guided Diffusion**  
Not central.

**CapRiCorn-1K / CLIP-CC-Bench**  
Mostly evaluation/captioning rather than editing syntax.

**EditYourself**  
Interesting if talking-head generation/manipulation becomes an actual renderer primitive for you, but not the first thing to study.

**Jump Cut Smoothing**  
A useful atomic operation, but too narrow to be the foundation of the format grammar.

**ShotVerse**  
More relevant to generative cinematic shot planning than your immediate deterministic reproduction problem.

# 14. The biggest architectural conclusion I reached

I think your video system should become **three stages, not two**.

Your existing system is:

```text
STAGE 1
Visual Observation
        ↓
STAGE 2
Composition Spec
```

For video I would use:

```text
VIDEO STAGE 1
Temporal Visual Observation
        ↓
VIDEO STAGE 2
Editing Grammar Induction
        ↓
VIDEO STAGE 3
Executable Composition / Rendering
```

And importantly:

### Stage 1 should NOT be “screenshots of the video.”

It should be a **temporal evidence package**.

Something like:

```text
video.mp4
    ↓
shot boundaries
    ↓
keyframes/contact sheets
    ↓
motion probes
    ↓
audio waveform / beats
    ↓
transcript / word timestamps
    ↓
OCR / typography regions
    ↓
VLM observations
```

Then Stage 1 produces something like:

```json
{
  "shot_id": "S07",
  "start_ms": 1840,
  "end_ms": 2760,

  "visual": {
    "shot_size": "medium",
    "camera_motion": "punch_in",
    "subject": "speaker",
    "composition": "centered"
  },

  "graphics": [
    {
      "type": "kinetic_text",
      "anchor": "lower_center",
      "onset_ms": 2030,
      "persistence_ms": 480
    }
  ],

  "audio": {
    "speech": true,
    "music_energy": "high"
  },

  "edit_context": {
    "previous_shot_relation": "semantic_contradiction",
    "cut_type": "hard_cut",
    "cut_function": "emphasis"
  }
}
```

Now you're building something the current Stage 2 cannot express.

# 15. Stage 2 should discover the **grammar**

This is where I think you can do something genuinely differentiated.

Not:

```yaml
use_punch_in: true
```

but:

```yaml
production_rule:
    name: ASSERTION_PUNCH

    when:
        utterance.function == ASSERTION
        emphasis_target != null

    compose:
        - establish_a_roll
        - delay_graphic(120ms)
        - punch_in(
              scale: 1.08,
              duration: 220ms,
              easing: ease_out
          )
        - reveal_keyword(
              onset: emphasis_target.word_boundary
          )

    constraints:
        - subject_identity_preserved
        - face_not_cropped
        - graphic_anchor == LOWER_CENTER
```

Now you have an **editing grammar**.

And that is something Remotion/FFmpeg/Hyperframes can all execute.

---

# 16. This also resolves the “Remotion vs FFmpeg vs Hyperframes vs DSPy” question

I would stop thinking of those as competing solutions.

They belong at different layers.

```text
                 FORMAT / HARNESS
                       │
                       ▼
              VISUAL SYNTAX IR
                       │
                       ▼
             TEMPORAL GRAMMAR
                       │
                       ▼
             COMPOSITION PLAN
                       │
          ┌────────────┼────────────┐
          ▼            ▼            ▼
       Remotion      FFmpeg      Hyperframes
```

And then:

```text
DSPy
```

belongs on the **reasoning side**:

```text
reference video
     ↓
observation program
     ↓
grammar induction
     ↓
composition program selection
     ↓
repair planning
```

Pydantic belongs around the contracts.

Embeddings belong where retrieval is useful.

Fine-tuning belongs **only once you have enough high-quality examples of the actual task**.

That is a much healthier architecture than asking one fine-tuned model to “edit like us.”

---

# 17. And this is where your five formats become incredibly important

I would **not build one giant universal video taxonomy first**.

Your five formats should act as five controlled experiments.

For each format:

```text
20-50 reference videos
       ↓
Stage 1 observations
       ↓
atomic editing operations
       ↓
recurring temporal motifs
       ↓
production rules
       ↓
format-specific grammar
```

Then you discover the intersection:

```text
UNIVERSAL VIDEO PRIMITIVES
```

and the differences:

```text
FORMAT-SPECIFIC GRAMMAR
```

For example:

```text
UNIVERSAL
    HARD_CUT
    J_CUT
    L_CUT
    PUNCH_IN
    TEXT_REVEAL
    IMAGE_OVERLAY
    SPLIT_SCREEN
    FREEZE
    SPEED_CHANGE

FORMAT A
    punch-in after claim
    screenshot proof
    aggressive caption

FORMAT B
    prolonged hold
    symbolic insert
    slow dissolve

FORMAT C
    dialogue isolation
    reaction beat
    visual silence

...
```

That is much more likely to generalize than directly learning “Format A”.

---

# 18. I would use Format01 as historical supervision

This is one of the most interesting things in your repository.

Your old Format01 scene library already has a surprisingly rich **semantic editing language**:

```text
HOOK
SETUP
CHALLENGE
```

# 19. My recommended reading order

If you are personally trying to master this field rather than merely delegate the research to an engineer, I would study them in this exact order:

### First pass - conceptual foundation

**1. VEU-Bench**  
Learn the vocabulary of editing operations and the recognition/reasoning/judging distinction. ([CVF Open Access](https://openaccess.thecvf.com/content/CVPR2025/html/Li_VEU-Bench_Towards_Comprehensive_Understanding_of_Video_Editing_CVPR_2025_paper.html?utm_source=chatgpt.com))

Learn to think in **editing components**, not merely video representations. ([arXiv](https://arxiv.org/abs/2403.16048?utm_source=chatgpt.com))

**3. AutoTransition**  
Learn why editing decisions depend on neighboring shots and multimodal context. ([arXiv](https://arxiv.org/abs/2207.13479?utm_source=chatgpt.com))

**4. V-Trans4Style**  
Learn how “production style” can become a measurable distribution of editing behavior rather than a prompt adjective. ([arXiv](https://arxiv.org/abs/2501.07983?utm_source=chatgpt.com))

### Second pass - architecture

**5. CutClaw**  
Study decomposition/planning/review rather than its specific implementation. ([arXiv](https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.29664?utm_source=chatgpt.com))

**6. Vidi**  
Study long-context multimodal retrieval and temporal grounding. ([arXiv](https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.15681?utm_source=chatgpt.com))

### Third pass - learned representation

**7. AutoCut**  
Study multimodal discretization and the idea of an intermediate executable token language. ([CatalyzeX](https://www.catalyzex.com/paper/autocut-end-to-end-advertisement-video?utm_source=chatgpt.com))

**8. OmniShotCut**  
Study reliable temporal boundary discovery. ([GitHub](https://github.com/UVA-Computer-Vision-Lab/OmniShotCut?utm_source=chatgpt.com))

### Fourth pass - evaluation

**9. IVEBench**  
Use it to think about the evaluation framework you'll need once the compiler exists. ([Hugging Face](https://huggingface.co/papers/2510.11647?utm_source=chatgpt.com))

**10. Self-SiMS**  
Only after that, because it belongs more to the retrieval/input-selection side that Format01 already addressed. ([arXiv](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.19027?utm_source=chatgpt.com))

# 🎬 The Conscious Movie Factory (CMF) 2.0: The Hybrid "Glass Box" Engine

**Master Overview & Engineering Blueprint (Final Revision)**

## 1. Executive Summary: The Industrialization of Creativity

The **Conscious Movie Factory (CMF)** represents a definitive break from the "Craftsman Model" of video production. For decades, video creation has been a manual, linear process of manipulation—a human operator dragging clips along a timeline, governed by intuition, limited by fatigue, and bound by the physical constraints of filming 1. The CMF replaces this with a process of **compilation**. We are not editing video; we are executing code.

Our mission is to operationalize **Digital Taylorism**. By decomposing the chaotic creative process into atomic, optimize-able units of logic, we transform video production from a service into a utility. This system does not rely on a single "Black Box" AI model to hallucinate a complete video from a vague prompt. Instead, it functions as a **"Glass Box" Factory**—a transparent, modular, and deterministic assembly line where every pixel, every sound wave, and every cut is the result of a specific, repeatable instruction.

The CMF operates on a **Sonic-First** hierarchy. We acknowledge the biological truth that sound is the primary driver of emotion. Therefore, the auditory landscape is architected *before* a single visual frame is generated. The video is forced to serve the audio, locking cuts to transient beats and emotional arcs with mathematical precision.

Crucially, the CMF 2.0 architecture democratizes high-end generative production. By validating the **"One-to-All Animation"** workflow on standard **RTX 4090** infrastructure via **Running Hub**, and utilizing **Natron** for professional compositing, we have proven that Hollywood-grade character consistency and motion do not require prohibitive H100 clusters. We have built a lean, scalable, and cost-effective engine capable of manufacturing "Main Character Energy" at industrial scale.

---

## 2. The Core Architecture: The "Hybrid Engine"

Previous iterations of generative video pipelines attempted to force a single tool (like ComfyUI) to handle generation, compositing, and editing. This resulted in fragile, unmanageable node graphs ("spaghetti monsters") that failed under the weight of complexity.

The **CMF 2.0 Architecture** introduces a "Hybrid Engine" that assigns the specific right tool to the right job. We separate the workflow into three distinct domains of labor:

### A. The Generator (The Miner)

- **Engine:** **ComfyUI** & **Wan 2.1 (One-to-All)** running on **Running Hub**.
- **Role:** To create the raw materials. This includes generating the "Immutable Stage" (backgrounds) via Z-Image/Flux and the "Generative Actor" (B-Roll) via the **One-to-All** model 2.
- **Efficiency:** By separating generation from compositing, we maximize the throughput of the GPU nodes, treating them as specialized "Fabrication Stations."

### B. The Fabricator (The Compositor)

- **Engine:** **Natron** (Open-Source Node-Based Compositor).
- **Role:** To assemble the raw materials into complex, broadcast-ready scenes. Natron is the engine for **C-Rolls** (Kinetic Typography, Motion Graphics) and **Master Effects** (Glitches, Z-Space Sandwiches). It replaces the manual "CapCut" work with automated, node-based rendering 3.
- **Output:** It bakes these effects into high-quality .mov or .mp4 "Scene Modules."

### C. The Assembler (The Editor)

- **Engine:** **MoviePy** (Python-based Non-Linear Editor).
- **Role:** To stitch the Scene Modules onto a timeline based on the Sonic Arc. The "Editor" is no longer a human; it is a Python script that reads a JSON manifest and places clips on the beat, every time, without error.

---

## 3. The "Unique Label" Data Protocol

To enable automation at this scale, we must eliminate ambiguity. In a manual workflow, an editor can look at a file named final\_final\_v2.mp4 and know what it is. In an automated factory, files must have **Unique Identity Labels**.

Every asset generated or procured by the CMF is assigned a **Universally Unique Identifier (UUID)** string that encodes its DNA. This allows for precise "Asset Curation" and organization of E-Rolls and D-Rolls.

The Naming Convention:

[PROJECT\_ID]\_[SCENE\_NUM]\_[ROLE]\_[TYPE]\_[VERSION].[EXT]

- **PROJECT\_ID:** PROJ\_001 (Links to the specific video project).
- **SCENE\_NUM:** SC\_04 (Links to the script line/timestamp).
- **ROLE:**
  - ICON (Generative B-Roll of the Client).
  - PERF (Performative B-Roll linked to Lyrics).
  - DROLL (Authentic "Dirty" Realism found footage).
  - EROLL (Cultural/Memetic clips).
  - CROLL (Kinetic Text/Graphics).
- **TYPE:** RAW (Uneffected) or FX (Composited).
- **VERSION:** v01, v02 (Allows for regeneration and A/B testing).

**Example:** PROJ\_Alpha\_SC\_03\_DROLL\_RAW\_v01.mp4

- *Translation:* "Project Alpha, Scene 3, Authentic Found Footage, Raw file, Version 1."

Why this matters:

This labeling system allows the Streamlit Console to function as a curation engine. The Director does not need to dig through folders. The system queries: "Show me all v01 candidates for SC\_03." It presents them side-by-side. The Director clicks one, and the system instantly tags it as SELECTED, moving it to the assembly manifest.

---

## 4. The 7-Stage Production Pipeline

### Stage 1: The Narrative Core (Extraction & Blueprinting)

This stage is the "Brain" of the operation. It transforms raw audio into a structured instruction set using LLM Agents.

- **Premise Mining:** The **Premise Hunter** agent scans raw transcripts using the **Viral Trinity Formula** (Surprise × Emotion × Specificity) to identify "Gold Nuggets"—high-arousal concepts that serve as the video's hook 4.
- **Script Composition:** The **Script Composer** assembles these nuggets into a cohesive 60-second narrative. Crucially, it operates under the **Verbatim Constraint**, ensuring the AI curates the client's actual words rather than hallucinating new text 5.
- **The Blueprint:** The **Blueprint Architect** generates the production\_blueprint.json 6. This "God Object" maps every second of the script to specific resources:
  - **Sonic Mapping:** Assigns a specific **Sonic Arc** (e.g., "The Rally," "The Divine Spark") 7.
  - **Visual Mapping:** Assigns a **Scene Template** (e.g., HOOK-4, SETUP-1) from the Master Library.
  - **Identity Mapping:** Determines whether the subject is the **Client** (Icon/Witness) or a generic **Character**.

### Stage 2: The Sonic Foundation (Musical Surgery & Lyrics)

This stage is where the "Musical Surgery" happens. We do not just "drop a song." We engineer the score.

- **Musical Surgery (The "Remix" Protocol):** The system takes a 4-minute song and automatically identifies the **Intro**, **Verse (Chill)**, and **Chorus (Climax)** sections using audio analysis (e.g., librosa/essentia).
  - It effectively "remixes" the song into a 60-second version: [Intro: 0-5s] -> [Verse: 5-45s] -> [Climax: 45-60s].
  - This creates the "Coherent Integration," ensuring the song's energy matches the video's arc without manual editing.
- **Lyric Generation & Analysis:** For Performative scenes, the system generates lyrics (via Suno or analyzes existing ones) and timestamps specific "quotable" lines.
- **The Librarian:** The system queries the local **SFX Library** (assets/sfx\_library/) to retrieve specific sound files (e.g., impact\_boom\_04.wav) triggered by keywords in the script 8.

### Stage 3: Asset Fabrication (The "Motion Harvest")

This is the most critical innovation of CMF 2.0. We move from "filming" to "harvesting." We do not ask the client to dance; we download the dance and inject the client.

- **The Motion Bank:** We curate a library of .pose files extracted from high-quality Artgrid/Filmpac stock footage using DWPose. These skeletons represent "perfect motion" (walking, pointing, celebrating).
- **The One-to-All Engine:** On **Running Hub**, we deploy the **One-to-All Animation** model (14B) on an RTX 4090 9.
  - **Input:** The Client's "Icon" Avatar (Static Image) + The Artgrid Motion Skeleton.
  - **Process:** The model "hallucinates" the client performing the motion. Because One-to-All uses **Self-Supervised Outpainting**, it can handle "Cross-Scale" transfer—generating legs if the avatar is a bust, or expanding the background if the camera moves—without breaking character consistency 10.
- **The Output:** A 4-second video of the client performing a professional action, generated in minutes on accessible hardware.

### Stage 4: C-Roll & VFX Fabrication (The Natron Factory)

This stage replaces manual editing effects. We have adapted the **Master Effects Library** (formerly CapCut instructions) into a library of **Natron Project Files (.ntp)**.

- **The Template System:** We maintain a library of .ntp files. Each file corresponds to a specific **Scene Template**:
  - **EFFECT\_M\_16.ntp:** "The Immersive Z-Space Sandwich" 11.
  - **EFFECT\_TR\_01.ntp:** "The Glitch Transition" 12.
  - **C\_ROLL\_KINETIC\_01.ntp:** "Kinetic Typography".
- **Variable Injection:** A Python script reads the Blueprint, opens the appropriate .ntp template, and programmatically swaps the "Read Node" file paths (Input Video/Text) to point to the Assets generated in Stage 3.
- **Rendering:** The system renders these composites out as finished "Scene Clips." This ensures that complex blurs, glows, and color grades are baked in with professional precision.

### Stage 5: Assembly & Engineering (The "Anchor Track" Protocol)

The "Editor" is a Python script using the **MoviePy** library. This stage is governed by the **Anchor Track Strategy** to prevent drift.

- **The Anchor Track (A1):** The system first lays down the cleaned, polished Voice Over audio on Track A1. This is the "Master Clock." The duration of the video is locked to this track.
- **The Slave Tracks:** All B-Roll, C-Roll, and Effect clips are "slaved" to the timestamps of A1. We do not place clips relative to each other; we place them relative to the master timestamp. If the script line "I failed" starts at 00:04:12, the corresponding B-Roll is hard-coded to snap to 00:04:12.
- **Logic-Based Mixing:** The system applies the **Volume Automation Map**.
  - **Rule A:** If A-Roll is present, the Music "Drums" stem is ducked by -12dB.
  - **Rule B:** If an SFX "Impact" occurs, the Music "Bass" stem is momentarily ducked to simulate side-chain compression.

### Stage 6: The Polish (Upscaling Station)

To optimize costs and speed, upscaling is decoupled from generation.

- **The Split Workflow:** We do not upscale inside the heavy One-to-All workflow.
- **The Polish Command:** Once the timeline is assembled or scenes are approved via Streamlit, the system triggers a secondary job on **Running Hub**.
- **The Upscaler:** A lightweight ComfyUI workflow (loading 4x-UltraSharp or RealESRGAN) takes the 720p/Native outputs and upscales them to 4K. This runs rapidly on standard GPUs, ensuring the heavy generation nodes remain free for the next batch.

### Stage 7: The Hybrid Output (The "Super-Assistant")

The CMF delivers a **Hybrid Output** that bridges automation and control:

1. **The Rendered Master (MP4):** A fully composited, color-graded, and mixed video file ready for immediate upload.
2. **The Project File (XML):** A **DaVinci Resolve XML** file. This file does *not* contain "baked" audio. It references the discrete stems and applies volume keyframes as metadata. This allows the human Director to open Resolve and tweak the mix or slip a cut in seconds, solving the "Vending Machine" problem of static AI outputs.

---

## 5. The Automated Captioning Engine (Minimalist Intelligence)

We reject the chaotic "Hormozi-style" captioning (flashing colors, emojis every second) in favor of a "Minimalist Intelligence" approach. The goal is retention through clarity, not over-stimulation.

**The "1-4 Word" Constraint:**

- The system uses **WhisperX** to generate word-level timestamps.
- **The Grouper:** A Python algorithm groups words into "visual phrases" of 1 to 4 words maximum.
  - *Bad:* "I went to the store and bought..." (Too long).
  - *Good:* "I went" / "to the store" / "and bought".
- **Output:** This creates a rapid, digestible reading rhythm (approx. 200-300ms per phrase) that keeps the eye moving without overwhelming the brain.

The "70/30" Automation Rule:

We automate variety without randomness using a strict probability distribution:

- **70% The Base (Minimalist Bold):**
  - **Style:** Clean, Sans-Serif font (e.g., Roboto, Montserrat). White text, slight drop shadow. Center or Lower-Third placement.
  - **Function:** Pure readability. No animation other than a simple appear/disappear.
  - **Logic:** The system applies this style by default to all connecting words ("the," "and," "but," "so").
- **30% The Accent (Creative Emphasis):**
  - **Style:** Larger Scale (1.2x), Accent Color (Brand Yellow/Red), or Kinetic Animation (Pop-in, Shake).
  - **Function:** Narrative Punctuation. Used to highlight the *keywords* that carry the meaning.
  - **Trigger Logic:** The script analyzer identifies keywords based on:
    1. **Semantic Value:** Nouns, Verbs, and Adjectives (e.g., "Failure," "Success," "Crushed").
    2. **Audio Intensity:** Words where the speaker's volume or pitch spikes (detected via librosa audio analysis).
  - **Execution:** When a keyword is detected, the system overrides the "Base" style with the "Accent" style for that specific phrase.

This ensures the captions feel "hand-crafted" and rhythmically aware, guiding the viewer's attention to the most important concepts rather than just flashing random colors.

([Adobe Research](https://research.adobe.com/publication/b-script-transcript-based-b-roll-video-editing-with-recommendations/?utm_source=chatgpt.com))

This maps beautifully onto your:

```text
FINAL SCRIPT
       ↓
WORD / PHRASE / EXPRESSION MOMENT
       ↓
B-ROLL OPPORTUNITY
```

rather than:

```text
VIDEO
  ↓
find visually similar place
  ↓
insert B-roll
```

That is a critical distinction.

### In your system, B-roll should probably become a **script-attached slot type**.

Something like:

```yaml
script_unit:
  id: S17
  text: "I realized I had been solving the wrong problem."

  semantic_function: realization

  authorized_visual_routes:
    - BROLL_CONTRADICTION
    - BROLL_SYMBOLIC
    - EROLL_MEMETIC
    - AROLL_PUNCH_IN

  sonic_state:
    energy: falling
    tension: high

  visual_priority:
    semantic_match: required
    format_style: required
```

Then your visual grammar determines how each route gets rendered.

That's *much* closer to what you're building.

# 3. Your own Format01 scene registry may be more important than VEU-Bench

This is the part I would emphasize most.

I went deeper into Format01 this time.

You don't merely have some old scenes lying around.

You have:

- 25 runtime scene templates

And the current Format01 documentation explicitly says that the scene builder is the real grammar source; the visual board is a specimen, not the authoritative scene atlas.

That's important.

> **semantic-to-editorial vocabulary.**

The missing work is to formalize its **visual syntax**.

So don't learn video editing grammar from scratch.

You already have part of it.

You need to expose what is implicit.

# 4. VEU-Bench still matters - but for a different reason

I still strongly recommend VEU-Bench.

But **not** because I think it should determine your editing timeline.

Its importance is that it gives you vocabulary for describing the *visible consequences* of editing:

- shot size
- camera properties
- shot motion
- cut type
- transition type
- inter-shot relations
- editing reasoning/judging

It explicitly organizes editing understanding into recognition, reasoning, and judging, and uses an ontology-based annotation process. ([CVPR Open Access](https://openaccess.thecvf.com/content/CVPR2025/html/Li_VEU-Bench_Towards_Comprehensive_Understanding_of_Video_Editing_CVPR_2025_paper.html?utm_source=chatgpt.com))

That makes it extremely useful for your **Stage 1 visual observation layer**.

In your language:

```text
REFERENCE VIDEO
      ↓
WHAT ACTUALLY HAPPENED?
      ↓
VEU-style observation vocabulary
      ↓
OUR CMF VISUAL SYNTAX
```

But not:

```text
REFERENCE VIDEO
      ↓
learn universal temporal policy
```

That's the distinction.

# 5. Edit3K becomes a very good paper for your "atomic primitive" layer

This one I still love for your project.

Edit3K deliberately separates the representation of **editing components** from the underlying media, with a large corpus covering thousands of editing components across effects, animation, transitions, filters, stickers and text. The authors explicitly focus on learning representations of the editing *action/component* rather than the raw visual content. ([arXiv](https://arxiv.org/abs/2403.16048?utm_source=chatgpt.com))

That maps almost exactly to your current primitive philosophy.

Instead of:

```text
this frame looks like this
```

you want:

```text
SOURCE
+
PUNCH_IN
+
TEXT_REVEAL
+
MASK
+
GLITCH
```

But now with your script-first authority:

```text
SCRIPT_FUNCTION
      ↓
ALLOWED EDITING COMPONENT
      ↓
EDIT3K-like atomic operation
      ↓
COMPOSITION IR
```

That is where I think Edit3K becomes very useful.

---

# 6. AutoTransition is not a foundation paper for you

This is where I would explicitly retract part of my previous advice.

AutoTransition is valuable.

It models transition recommendation from neighboring shots plus audio, using multimodal retrieval and sequential context. ([arXiv](https://arxiv.org/abs/2207.13479?utm_source=chatgpt.com))

But its worldview starts from:

```text
shot A
shot B
audio
→
transition
```

Whereas yours should start from:

```text
script event
semantic relation
sonic relation
visual relation
→
eligible transition
```

So I would use AutoTransition **later**, specifically for your multimodal transition engine.

And yes:

> **I agree with you that multimodal transitions are extremely relevant.**

But I would define them as a **conditional realization operator**, not as the temporal governor.

For example:

```text
SCRIPT:
"Then everything changed."

SEMANTIC:
TURNING_POINT

SONIC:
rising tension → impact

MEDIA:
A-roll → E-roll

TRANSITION CANDIDATES:
    smash_cut
    hard_cut
    match_cut
    graphic_hit

FORMAT:
Format03

VISUAL SYNTAX:
    punch-in
    contrast shift
    impact typography
```

Now the transition is selected from a **semantic + sonic + visual context**.

That's much more interesting than generic transition recommendation.

---

# 7. V-Trans4Style is downstream, not upstream

Same correction here.

V-Trans4Style is useful because it treats production style as a sequence/distribution of transitions and introduces style conditioning. That's useful for your **format fidelity** question.

But I would not let it define the architecture.

Your architecture should be:

```text
SCRIPT
   ↓
EDITORIAL DECISION
   ↓
FORMAT
   ↓
VISUAL REALIZATION
```

not:

```text
TARGET STYLE
   ↓
transition sequence
```

So V-Trans4Style is a **style-realization research paper**, not your foundational theory of temporal editing. ([ECVA](https://www.ecva.net/papers/eccv_2022/papers_ECCV/papers/136980282.pdf?utm_source=chatgpt.com))

---

# 8. There is another paper you should absolutely read: AVscript

I would add **AVscript: Accessible Video Editing with Audio-Visual Scripts** to your curriculum.

It creates a text/script representation that embeds visual content, visual errors and speech so users can navigate and edit video through an audio-visual script rather than being forced to reason directly over the timeline. ([arXiv](https://arxiv.org/abs/2302.14117?utm_source=chatgpt.com))

This matters because it reinforces something you're independently converging toward:

> **The script can be the human-readable control surface for the temporal system.**

Your future CMF could essentially be:

```text
SCRIPT
───────────────────────────────
01  "I used to think..."
    A-ROLL
    ↓
02  "But then I realized..."
    TURNING_POINT
    ↓
03  "Here's what changed..."
    B-ROLL / PROOF
    ↓
04  "And this is the result..."
    E-ROLL
```

with the visual realization attached to script nodes.

The underlying timeline becomes an **implementation**, not the authoring language.

That's very CMF.

---

# 9. There is an even older research lineage you should investigate

This was a particularly interesting find.

There is older work on **automatic cinematography / video generation from discourse structures**, where an audio commentary/discourse representation drives:

- image retrieval
- shot segmentation
- camera movement
- transition selection
- synchronization with spoken commentary

rather than the video dictating the narrative structure. ([ScienceDirect](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0004370205000226?utm_source=chatgpt.com))

That research lineage is surprisingly close to your 2025 CMF philosophy.

And I think it is worth revisiting because it asks the deeper question:

> **How do you translate discourse structure into cinematic realization?**

That's fundamentally your problem.


So a video syntax unit might be:

```yaml
unit_id: TURNING_POINT_03
script_ref: script.line.27
semantic_function: revelation

roll:
  preferred: E
  fallback: B

sonic:
  energy: rising
  transient: true
  speech_emphasis: true

visual:
  bbox:
    subject_zone: 0.15,0.05,0.70,0.85
    text_zone: 0.08,0.68,0.84,0.20

  why:
    subject: "force attention onto contradiction"

```

# One subtle correction I'd make to your statement

You said:

> “Temporal editing is semantic.”

I would say:

> **Temporal authority is semantic; temporal behavior is multimodal.**

That's the formulation I would put into the architecture.

Because timing has several sources:

```text
SCRIPT
   ↓
semantic boundaries

AUDIO
   ↓
rhythm / transient / phrase / breath / emphasis

MEDIA
   ↓
available motion / shot duration / continuity

FORMAT
   ↓
allowed pacing / repetition / density

VISUAL SYNTAX
   ↓
animation duration / reveal duration / hold duration
```

But **only the script/semantic program gets to decide what the edit is trying to accomplish.**

That preserves your constitutional boundary.

# And now I think the five formats should be studied differently

For each of your five formats, I would **not ask**:

I would ask:

Then:

### Semantic taxonomy

```text
WHAT DOES THE SCRIPT SAY?
```

### Editorial taxonomy

```text
WHAT SHOULD THE EDITOR DO?
```

### Roll taxonomy

```text
WHICH MEDIA ROLE SHOULD SERVE IT?
```

### Sonic taxonomy

```text
WHAT DOES AUDIO DO?
```

### Visual taxonomy

```text
HOW IS THAT DECISION RENDERED?
```

### Transition taxonomy

```text
HOW DOES ONE EDITORIAL STATE BECOME THE NEXT?
```

### Execution taxonomy

```text
HOW DOES THE RUNTIME ACTUALLY BUILD IT?
```

That, to me, is the proper **CMF Editing Ontology**.

# The deepest opportunity

I think your real research problem is not:

> “Can an AI edit video?”

That's already crowded.

It is:

> **Can we represent a proprietary editorial language as a deterministic, inspectable compiler between script intent and audiovisual realization?**

And that is a much more interesting problem.

Because then your eventual system can learn:

```text
               SCRIPT
                  ↓
          semantic program
                  ↓
         editorial operators
                  ↓
          media-role routing
                  ↓
        sonic visual coupling
                  ↓
        visual syntax operators
                  ↓
           transition rules
                  ↓
         executable composition
```

And your renderer becomes almost boring.

That's good.

The **intelligence lives in the grammar**.

Your old A/B/C/E-roll architecture, scene registry, effect registry, sonic foundation, anchor-track protocol and current script-owned `VideoEditProgram` are not obsolete ideas. They are pieces of a compiler architecture that were previously expressed operationally rather than as a formal ontology.

# 1. “Activated reasons” should sit above everything

This is the key insight I would formalize.

A video does not become compelling merely because:

- it cuts every 2.7 seconds,
- it has kinetic captions,
- it uses B-roll,
- it has a particular camera movement,
- it has a particular transition,
- it uses a trending sound.

Those are **realization mechanisms**.

The reason the video works is deeper.

Something in the content causes the viewer to:

- anticipate,
- identify,
- recognize themselves,
- feel tension,
- wonder,
- compare,
- laugh,
- fear,
- desire,
- understand,
- feel relief,
- experience novelty,
- experience status,
- experience belonging,
- receive evidence,
- resolve uncertainty,
- etc.

Your term **Activated Reason** is actually a very useful abstraction for this.

I would make it the highest semantic-level object in the system.

Something like:

```text
ACTIVATED REASON
       │
       ├── cognitive
       ├── emotional
       ├── identity
       ├── curiosity
       ├── surprise
       ├── tension
       ├── recognition
       ├── social
       ├── aesthetic
       └── entertainment
```

Then:

```text
ACTIVATED REASON
       ↓
SEMANTIC / NARRATIVE MECHANISM
       ↓
SONIC ORCHESTRATION
       ↓
EDITORIAL / SCENE DECISION
       ↓
ROLL SELECTION
       ↓
VISUAL SYNTAX
       ↓
EFFECT / TRANSITION
       ↓
EXECUTION
```

That is the hierarchy I think you've been trying to describe for years.

---

# 2. This resolves our earlier disagreement about temporal grammar

I would now make a stronger statement:

> **The timeline is not a semantic object. It is an execution projection of semantic + sonic decisions.**

That is an important distinction.

The script determines:

> **what must happen and why.**

The sonic architecture determines:

> **how the experience breathes through time.**

The scene grammar determines:

> **what editorial mode is appropriate.**

The roll grammar determines:

> **what kind of media should carry the meaning.**

The visual syntax determines:

> **how that media should be visually composed.**

The execution IR determines:

> **exactly how it is instantiated at frame/time level.**

So:

```text
              WHY
       Activated Reason
              ↓
             WHAT
      Semantic Program
              ↓
             HOW
       Sonic Program
              ↓
       Editorial Program
              ↓
         Scene Program
              ↓
         Roll Program
              ↓

```

This is much cleaner than calling the whole thing “editing grammar.”

There are **multiple grammars**.

# 3. I think your biggest missing piece is actually the Editorial Program

Look at what you just described.

Your script gives you meaning.

- story arc,

For example:

```text
SCRIPT:

ACTIVATED REASONS:
    curiosity
    identity tension
    self-recognition

SEMANTIC FUNCTION:
    setup / false belief

    establish familiarity

TRANSITION:

```

Notice what happened.

That is an observable pattern, not a causal law.

The actual variable is closer to:

> **rate of meaningful state change**

rather than simply:

There can be a 9-second static shot with enormous activation.

And there can be 9 cuts in 3 seconds with almost zero meaningful engagement.

```text
PACING
├── semantic change rate
├── visual change rate

├── emotional change rate
└── information-reveal rate
```

Now you can have:

```text
high sonic
low emotional
```

```text
strong emotional
```

Those are completely different experiences.

Purpose:

Did the output preserve the intended experiential mechanism?

### Editorial Fidelity

Did the media operations serve the semantic/activation intent correctly?

### Sonic Fidelity

Did rhythm, energy, dynamics and musical structure produce the intended experiential timing?

### Visual-Syntax Fidelity

Did the output obey the format's spatial, graphic, compositional and motion grammar?

### Format Fidelity

Does the result *feel like a member of this format family*?

### Temporal Coherence

Do the operations occur at sensible moments relative to speech, sonic events and scene states?

### Execution Fidelity

Did the runtime faithfully execute the approved program?

Yes. I think we have finally arrived at the right level of abstraction.

After going back into the repository rather than reasoning from the older CMF description alone, I would make one major change to the whole research program:

> **Do not build a “video-editing curriculum.” Build a curriculum for the CMF editorial language.**

Because your problem is much narrower and much more interesting.

You already have the content-production doctrine. You already have the interview-first pipeline. You already have the script authority. You already have the sonic layer. You already have the scene registry. You already have A/B/C/E roles. You already have effects. You already have a working visual-syntax observation/compiler subsystem. The missing piece is the **formal theory behind the composition of a Scene** and how that composition consistently realizes a semantic function across formats.

That is what the 33 subjects should teach you.

# First: I agree with your “80-99% is composition” thesis

Looking at the actual repository, Format01 has **60 scene templates across 17 scene families**. A scene record already contains things such as:

- scene family/type
- constituent elements
- a visual recipe
- effects

And the Format01 syntax tooling explicitly asks for:

- syntax ID
- BBOX + WHY
- pose/gaze plan
- sonic plan
- invariants
- variants
- failure modes
- runtime plan

So the architecture you were building six months ago was already saying:

> **A scene is a structured composition, not merely a timestamped clip.**

That is the idea I'd promote to the top of the curriculum.

Even better, the existing scene registry already contains things like:

> “A-Roll statement + matching B-Roll”

> “A-Roll setup → L-Cut → found clip”

> “A-Roll names enemy → aggressive C-Roll takedown”

> “confident A-Roll + echo of past vulnerability”

> “C-Roll split-screen”

That means your old system already contains the beginnings of an **editorial grammar**.

The problem isn't that you lacked a grammar.

The problem is that the grammar was mostly **implicit inside scene recipes**.

The research job is to make it explicit, canonical, composable and executable.

---

# Second: I would simplify the pipeline exactly as you suggested

I would now define the core production logic as:

```text
INTERVIEW
   ↓
TRANSCRIPT
   ↓
SEMANTIC PROGRAM
   ↓
SONIC ORCHESTRATION
   ↓
SCENE SELECTION
   ↓
SCENE COMPOSITION
   ↓
VISUAL SYNTAX
   ↓
EXECUTABLE COMPOSITION IR
   ↓
RENDER
```

And I would **not** introduce a giant independent “temporal grammar” between script and scene.

The script is the semantic authority.

The sonic program provides the experiential timing field.

The scene determines the compositional treatment.

The visual syntax determines the spatial/graphic realization.

The runtime executes.

That is enough.

B-Script is particularly aligned with this philosophy because it makes transcript structure the editing surface and recommends B-roll position/content against that transcript rather than making the timeline the primary semantic interface. ([Bernd Huber](https://berndhuber.github.io/bscript/?utm_source=chatgpt.com))

Likewise, RoughCut is important because its editing idioms operate on **script-derived structure** rather than asking the system to infer a universal timeline from finished videos. ([Stanford Graphics](https://graphics.stanford.edu/papers/roughcut/files/roughcut-small.pdf?utm_source=chatgpt.com))

---

# Third: your formats should be treated as **scene grammars**

This is probably the most important conclusion from everything you've said.

You have:

```text
FORMAT 01
FORMAT 02
FORMAT 03
FORMAT 04
FORMAT 05
```

And each format has:

```text
THEME
SCENE REGISTRY
SCENE TAXONOMY
ALLOWED CONTENT TYPES
VISUAL SYNTAX FAMILY
EFFECT FAMILY
```

That is much better than saying:

> “Format 01 has a certain editing style.”

I would define:

> **A Format is a stable editorial language with a bounded vocabulary of Scenes.**

Therefore:

```text
FORMAT
   ↓
SCENE REGISTRY
   ↓
SCENE
   ↓
COMPONENTS
   ↓
VISUAL SYNTAX
```

This also explains why **theme** and **format** need to remain separate.

Theme is the recognizable skin/world.

Format is the learned structural language.

Semantics are what the specific episode is saying.

That distinction is extremely useful.

Research on schema-based television reception supports the intuition that viewers bring learned cognitive schemas to recurring media forms; genre/form familiarity can shape how meaning is interpreted. ([ScienceDirect](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/0304422X9290010Z?utm_source=chatgpt.com))

And the familiarity point is directionally supported by the broader mere-exposure literature: repeated exposure can increase familiarity and liking, although the relationship is not simply monotonic and should not be treated as a universal law. A large meta-analysis found a nonlinear relationship rather than “more repetition is always better.” ([PubMed](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/28263645/?utm_source=chatgpt.com))

So I would absolutely study this, but I would phrase the design hypothesis carefully:

> **A consistent format can reduce the amount of structural interpretation a returning viewer has to perform, while allowing novelty to live inside the semantic content.**

That is a much safer proposition than claiming “format familiarity always increases retention.”

---

# The 33-subject curriculum

I would organize the 33 subjects into **7 schools**.

This is not a generic film-school curriculum.

It is the curriculum for becoming the person who can eventually specify and engineer your CMF editorial language.

---

# SCHOOL I - SEMANTIC → VISUAL COMMUNICATION

These are the most important subjects.

### 01. Semantic-to-Visual Mapping

How an abstract proposition becomes a concrete visual representation.

Study:

- literal representation
- illustrative representation
- metaphor
- analogy
- symbolic representation
- evidence
- contrast
- externalization
- visual explanation

This is the theoretical foundation of your scene system.

Your core question:

> “What is the best visual representation of this exact semantic function?”

This is where your existing C-roll philosophy belongs.

---

### 02. Visual Rhetoric

Learn how visual forms make arguments.

Study:

- emphasis
- contrast
- juxtaposition
- comparison
- hierarchy
- framing
- omission
- proximity
- scale
- visual metaphor

This is critical because your scenes aren't merely decorative.

They **make meaning**.

---

### 03. Visual Narrativity

Study how an image or composition can imply:

- before/after
- cause/effect
- conflict
- transformation
- status
- identity
- consequence
- intention

This is especially relevant to your C-rolls and silent-dialogue format.

Research on visual narrativity specifically argues that still visual content can carry narrative structure and reviews this through the lens of narrative transportation. ([the University of Bath's research portal](https://researchportal.bath.ac.uk/en/publications/narrate-act-and-resonate-to-tell-a-visual-story-a-systematic-revi/?utm_source=chatgpt.com))

---

### 04. Narrative Transportation & Viewer Immersion

This is the first psychological subject I would study deeply.

Transportation is not just “attention.”

It concerns cognitive, emotional and imagery involvement in a narrative and has a substantial literature around media enjoyment and persuasion. ([Wiley Online Library](https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1111/j.1468-2885.2004.tb00317.x?utm_source=chatgpt.com))

This is where your **Activated Reasons** idea should be connected to established theory.

You don't need to adopt “transportation” as your product ontology.

But you should understand it.

---

### 05. Viewer Identification & Character Connection

Study:

- identification
- empathy
- perspective taking
- social cognition
- self-relevance
- character liking

This is especially important because your entire system is **interview-first**.

Your raw material is a human being speaking.

That means the person is not merely A-roll footage.

The person is one of the semantic mechanisms of the content.

Transportation/identification research explicitly distinguishes these forms of engagement and their different antecedents. ([Taylor & Francis Online](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/abs/10.1080/23808985.2015.11735255?utm_source=chatgpt.com))

---

# SCHOOL II - COMPOSITION & VISUAL PERCEPTION

This is where I expect you'll spend enormous time.

### 06. Spatial Composition

Study:

- balance
- tension
- symmetry
- asymmetry
- scale
- alignment
- margins
- visual weight
- negative space
- dominance

This is your core Stage 1 subject.

---

### 07. Visual Hierarchy

Study how viewers determine:

> “What should I look at first?”

Then:

> “What should I look at second?”

This becomes part of your BBOX + WHY language.

---

### 08. Gestalt Grouping

Study:

- proximity
- similarity
- common region
- continuation
- closure
- figure-ground
- common fate
- synchrony

These are not just design-school principles. Modern vision research has revisited grouping and figure-ground organization extensively. ([PubMed](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/22845751/?utm_source=chatgpt.com))

This should directly influence your composition ontology.

---

### 09. Attention & Visual Salience

Study:

- bottom-up salience
- top-down attention
- gaze cues
- motion salience
- contrast
- faces
- text
- object importance

There is strong empirical work linking movie editing and composition to viewers' gaze distributions. ([PubMed](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/36002630/?utm_source=chatgpt.com))

This is highly relevant to your “composition is 80%” claim.

---

### 10. Eye Tracking & Gaze Behavior

Not because you're going to install eye trackers tomorrow.

Because you need to understand:

> **How do we know that a composition actually guides the eye the way we think it does?**

Study:

- fixation
- saccade
- scanpath
- gaze concentration
- attentional capture
- gaze following

The film-editing literature gives you a bridge from composition/editing decisions to measured viewer gaze. ([PubMed](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/36002630/?utm_source=chatgpt.com))

---

### 11. Perceptual Continuity & Edit Blindness

This is a small but important subject.

Study why viewers can miss significant visual changes when edits coincide with attention shifts or motion.

“Edit blindness” research is directly relevant to understanding why some cuts disappear perceptually while others become salient events. ([BOP Serials](https://bop.unibe.ch/JEMR/article/view/2264?utm_source=chatgpt.com))

This helps you avoid confusing:

> visible cut

with

> perceived change.

---

### 12. Cognitive Load & Information Density

Study:

- working-memory limitations
- extraneous processing
- clutter
- competing signals
- cognitive load
- information density

Mayer's multimedia-learning work is extremely relevant to C-roll composition because it formalizes principles such as coherence, signaling, redundancy, spatial contiguity and temporal contiguity as ways to reduce unnecessary cognitive processing. ([Cambridge University Press](https://www.cambridge.org/core/books/abs/cambridge-handbook-of-multimedia-learning/principles-for-reducing-extraneous-processing-in-multimedia-learning-coherence-signaling-redundancy-spatial-contiguity-and-temporal-contiguity-principles/C98AB3A6CE760DD63C048936EA0B3B44?utm_source=chatgpt.com))

This is probably one of the most important bridges between your **visual syntax** and your **semantic communication**.

---

# SCHOOL III - THE SCENE AS A LANGUAGE

This is the heart of the curriculum.

### 13. Scene Grammar

Study the scene as:

```text
semantic purpose
+
constituent components
+
composition
+
constraints
```

This is where your 60-template registry becomes formal grammar rather than a library of examples.

---

### 14. Scene Taxonomy Design

Study how to classify scenes without creating useless categories.

Learn:

- orthogonality
- mutual exclusivity
- hierarchical classification
- compositional taxonomy
- family/subfamily design
- canonical naming
- taxonomic collapse

Your goal:

> every scene should have a clear identity and a bounded purpose.

---

### 15. Scene Ontology

Taxonomy says:

> “What classes exist?”

Ontology says:

> “How do these classes relate?”

You need both.

For example:

```text
PROOF
  is-a EVIDENCE_SCENE

PROOF_WITH_SCREEN
  is-a PROOF

PROOF_WITH_SCREEN
  contains C_ROLL
```

This will become important when you build your scene compiler.

---

### 16. Scene Components & Compositionality

Study how scenes can be constructed from reusable parts.

For example:

```text
SCENE
├── A_ROLL
├── B_ROLL
├── C_ROLL
├── E_ROLL
├── TEXT
├── FRAME
└── EFFECT
```

but without assuming every scene supports every role.

This is where your existing scene registry has enormous value.

---

### 17. A-Roll Grammar

Study what the talking head is allowed to do.

Your intuition here is already strong:

> A-roll should usually have the least visual interference.

Formalize:

- jump cuts
- reframing
- punch-ins
- reaction emphasis
- silence
- pause
- gaze
- crop
- cadence

The purpose is not flashy editing.

It is **semantic preservation**.

---

### 18. B-Roll Grammar

Study B-roll as:

> **evidence / illustration / context**

rather than “pretty footage.”

Taxonomize:

- evidentiary
- illustrative
- contextual
- metaphorical
- emotional
- environmental
- archival
- procedural

And define what counts as a *good semantic match*.

B-Script is highly relevant here because it explicitly treats B-roll placement and content as a transcript-conditioned editing problem. ([Bernd Huber](https://berndhuber.github.io/bscript/?utm_source=chatgpt.com))

---

### 19. C-Roll Grammar

This is probably **your most strategically important subject**.

C-roll is where the whole carousel/supervisual visual-syntax program converges into video.

Study:

- diagrammatic composition
- conceptual visualization
- typographic systems
- mixed-media composition
- annotation
- layering
- comparison
- transformation
- spatial explanation
- visual metaphor

Your current Stage 1/Stage 2 experience is immediately transferable here.

---

### 20. E-Roll Grammar

Study:

- interruption
- humor
- cultural reference
- meme
- surprise
- emotional punctuation
- archetypal imagery
- irony

The important distinction:

> E-roll exists partly to alter the **viewer state**, not merely to explain the script.

That's where entertainment grammar belongs.

---

# SCHOOL IV - VISUAL SYNTAX

This is your biggest technical curriculum.

### 21. BBOX + WHY

I would make this a formal discipline.

Not merely:

```text
x,y,w,h
```

but:

```text
region
role
relationship
purpose
constraint
```

This is exactly where your existing carousel work is ahead of most generic video systems.

---

### 22. Spatial Relationships

Study:

- containment
- adjacency
- overlap
- alignment
- opposition
- attachment
- hierarchy
- separation
- anchoring

This is what converts bounding boxes into **composition semantics**.

---

### 23. Typography as Visual Syntax

Study:

- hierarchy
- font personality
- scale
- line length
- tracking
- weight
- alignment
- emphasis
- placement
- motion
- reading order

Don't think “captions.”

Think:

> **typographic objects inside a scene.**

---

### 24. Motion Grammar

Not “video effects.”

Study:

- reveal
- enter
- exit
- displacement
- scale
- pan
- tracking
- transformation
- accumulation
- reset

The question is:

> What does the movement communicate?

---

### 25. Effects as Scene Modifiers

This is precisely where I agree with your correction.

Effects shouldn't be their own conceptual world.

They belong **inside Scene realization**.

So study:

```text
scene
  ↓
effect eligibility
  ↓
effect selection
  ↓
effect parameters
```

rather than:

```text
video
  ↓
random effects
```

Your old effect registry should become a constrained **scene-bound effect registry**.

---

# SCHOOL V - SONIC ORCHESTRATION

This deserves a serious place, but I would keep it subordinate to semantic intent.

### 26. Music & Emotion

Study how music affects emotional response.

Audio-visual congruence research shows that congruent visual presentation can intensify emotional responses to music relative to audio alone. ([PubMed Central (PMC)](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6542535/?utm_source=chatgpt.com))

This supports your conviction that sound isn't merely an accompaniment layer.

---

### 27. Sonic Arc Design

Study:

- buildup
- release
- tension
- plateau
- acceleration
- deceleration
- climax
- resolution

Then map:

```text
SCRIPT ARC
      ↓
SONIC ARC
```

This should become a formal CMF object.

---

### 28. Audio-Visual Congruence & Contrast

Study not just matching:

> happy music + happy visual

but deliberate mismatch:

> calm audio + chaotic visual

> dramatic audio + mundane visual

> melancholy audio + ironic E-roll

This is especially important for Format01-style scenes like your “Stylized Mismatch.”

---

### 29. Sonic Editing Events

Study:

- beat
- transient
- phrase boundary
- downbeat
- pause
- vocal onset
- lyric onset
- musical accent

Not to create a mechanical “cut on beat” system.

Rather:

> **Which visual opportunities naturally become salient because of sonic structure?**

That is the better formulation of your sonic-first philosophy.

---

# SCHOOL VI - FORMAT, THEME & RECOGNIZABILITY

This is where your “show people come back to the format” intuition gets formalized.

### 30. Format Grammar vs Theme Grammar

This is a crucial conceptual distinction.

**Format:**

> what kinds of scenes and compositions repeatedly occur.

**Theme:**

> the recognizable visual/cultural world in which those scenes are expressed.

Study them separately.

---

### 31. Genre, Schema & Viewer Expectations

Study how viewers use learned schemas to interpret recurring media forms.

Research on television reception has explicitly examined genre as a cognitive structure involving schemas and frames used during interpretation. ([ScienceDirect](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/0304422X9290010Z?utm_source=chatgpt.com))

This is directly relevant to your:

> “once someone learns the format, it becomes easier to consume.”

---

### 32. Familiarity, Mere Exposure & Recognition

Study this carefully because your intuition may be partly right but the psychology is more nuanced.

Repeated exposure can increase liking/familiarity, but the effect can be nonlinear and depends on conditions. The 2017 meta-analysis is particularly useful because it pushes back against simplistic “more repetition = more liking” interpretations. ([PubMed](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/28263645/?utm_source=chatgpt.com))

The engineering takeaway I'd make is:

> **Consistency should create recognizability without exhausting novelty.**

That is a much better design principle.

---

### 33. Format Fidelity & Comparative Evaluation

This is the final subject because it ties everything together.

You need to learn how to compare:

```text
REFERENCE
vs
GENERATED OUTPUT
```

across separate dimensions:

```text
semantic fidelity
scene fidelity
composition fidelity
visual-syntax fidelity
sonic fidelity
format fidelity
theme fidelity
execution fidelity
```

Not:

> “Does it look similar?”

But:

> **“Did the system reproduce the language?”**

That is your actual endgame.

---

# And there is a very important omission in my earlier recommendations

I would **not** make “learn video generation models” part of this first curriculum.

Not yet.

I would also not make:

- fine-tuning
- diffusion
- video-token models
- agent swarms
- multimodal foundation models
- latent representations
- embeddings
- DSPy

core research subjects at this stage.

Those are implementation options.

Your ontology should be stable **before** you decide which model architecture implements it.

---

# The papers I'd put beside the curriculum

The first research shelf would now be:

### Script / scene reasoning

**RoughCut** - script → editing idioms → shot decisions. This is probably your most conceptually relevant paper. ([Stanford Graphics](https://graphics.stanford.edu/papers/roughcut/files/roughcut-small.pdf?utm_source=chatgpt.com))

**B-Script** - transcript → B-roll recommendation/editing. ([arXiv](https://arxiv.org/abs/1902.11216?utm_source=chatgpt.com))

**AVscript** - script-centered audiovisual representation. ([arXiv](https://arxiv.org/abs/2302.14117?utm_source=chatgpt.com))

### Visual/editing ontology

**VEU-Bench** - a good external vocabulary for observing editing components and evaluating recognition/reasoning/judgment. It explicitly organizes 19 tasks into those three levels and uses an ontology-based annotation pipeline. ([arXiv](https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.17828?utm_source=chatgpt.com))

**Edit3K** - especially useful for your atomic component/effect vocabulary. It isolates editing components from raw content and provides a large component corpus. ([arXiv](https://arxiv.org/abs/2403.16048?utm_source=chatgpt.com))

### Perception

**Where to Look at the Movies** - composition/editing ↔ gaze. ([PubMed](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/36002630/?utm_source=chatgpt.com))

**Edit Blindness** - why viewers don't necessarily consciously perceive every edit. ([BOP Serials](https://bop.unibe.ch/JEMR/article/view/2264?utm_source=chatgpt.com))

**Impact of Continuity Editing on Event Segmentation** - why editing can bridge perceptual discontinuities while preserving narrative comprehension. ([PubMed Central (PMC)](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3208769/?utm_source=chatgpt.com))

### Cognitive communication

**Mayer / Multimedia Learning** - coherence, signaling, redundancy, spatial/temporal contiguity. This is unusually relevant to C-roll. ([Cambridge University Press](https://www.cambridge.org/core/books/abs/cambridge-handbook-of-multimedia-learning/principles-for-reducing-extraneous-processing-in-multimedia-learning-coherence-signaling-redundancy-spatial-contiguity-and-temporal-contiguity-principles/C98AB3A6CE760DD63C048936EA0B3B44?utm_source=chatgpt.com))

**Gestalt / perceptual grouping** - for composition ontology. ([PubMed](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/22845751/?utm_source=chatgpt.com))

### Engagement

**Narrative Transportation** - for the psychological side of your Activated Reasons doctrine. ([Wiley Online Library](https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1111/j.1468-2885.2004.tb00317.x?utm_source=chatgpt.com))

**Transportation vs Identification** - useful for separating emotional immersion from character connection. ([Taylor & Francis Online](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/abs/10.1080/23808985.2015.11735255?utm_source=chatgpt.com))

Not because prose is better than JSON, and not because agents should be allowed to improvise freely, but because **composition itself is often easier to discover iteratively than to specify perfectly on the first pass**.

# The architecture I would use

I would introduce an **Evolutionary Composition Loop**:

```text id="evo_loop"
SEMANTIC INTENT
      ↓
PRIMITIVE SELECTION
      ↓
DRAFT COMPOSITION
      ↓
VISUALIZATION / RENDER
      ↓
CRITIQUE
      ↓
STRUCTURAL REVISION
      ↓
RENDER
      ↓
VALIDATION
      ↓
CANONICAL COMPOSITION
```

The crucial thing is that the system does **not** jump directly:

```text
semantic intent → final JSON
```

Instead:

```text
semantic intent
    ↓
candidate composition
    ↓
draft
    ↓
visual evidence
    ↓
revision
    ↓
canonical IR
```

That is much closer to how a human designer actually works.

---

This is the important part.

I would create **two representations**:

Loose, generative, revisable.

It can look like:

```text

A smaller evidence image sits behind it.
The keyword floats near the center.
The lower area remains intentionally empty."
```

Or even:

```text

evidence behind
keyword center
dark background

```

Or a structured sketch:

```json

  "subject": "left",
  "evidence": "rear_layer",
  "keyword": "center",
  "negative_space": "bottom"
}
```

All three can coexist.

Strict.

```json
{
```

### Mutator

Changes the smallest set of parameters needed to resolve the critique.

Determines whether the composition is legal.

Converts the winner into canonical IR.

That is a much cleaner agentic system.
